remainingEvidence: Presence-typing `interceptable` changed OperationDescriptor.toData()'s canonical bytes: a withheld capability emitted `interceptable: false` before and emits no key now. That is the point of C13-FACET-CAPABILITY-ABSENCE — the withheld meaning must have exactly one encoding — but it is a wire-format change, and thirteen sites digest descriptor bytes.

TWO of those thirteen feed a DURABLE identity. My first enumeration said one and was wrong; CompactionConcept traced the second after being asked to check, and I verified every link in it before recording this. The first is: src/composition/mediation-identity.ts#DerivedMediationIdentities.invocation commits `descriptor: Digest.sha256(encodeCanonicalJson(request.descriptor.toData()))` into the InvocationId. So every Invocation minted against an Operation that withholds interception — which is every Operation that never declared the capability — now derives a different id from the same intent. test/composition/mediation-identity.test.ts says so in its own words: these identifiers name records already in storage, the derivation is a wire format, and a diff is a migration question rather than a refactor.

The second durable derivation is src/agents/runs/executor.ts#modelInputCommitId. executor.ts:1460 boundOperationData embeds the whole of descriptor.toData() in each catalog entry; TurnModelInput.toData() carries that catalog at :477; :1156 puts TurnModelInput.encode(record) into the content-addressed ContentStore; :1490 derives the RunCommitId as `model-input:${sha256({document, parent})}`. So the same intent against the same head now yields a different modelInput RunCommitId. Verified by execution rather than by reading: the canonical catalog entry digests to 731926782a5a6a30 with `interceptable: false` present and to 66b7d2f09188300b with the key absent.

That second fork reaches a recovery path rather than only a record at rest, which makes it the more serious half. SS5.6 settles an unknown outcome by re-reading the exact commit its content and parent derive, so a host that dispatched, crashed before recording the outcome, and retries ACROSS this change computes a different commit id for the identical request, fails to find its own prior commit, and dispatches a second model call - the double call C13-TURN-MODEL-INPUT-DURABLE-BEFORE-DISPATCH exists to prevent. It is the default path, not an edge: every Operation that never declared interception has different descriptor bytes now. So the open question extends to run.commit records of kind modelInput, which SS5.2 makes undeletable, and nobody holds an inventory establishing whether any exist.

The remaining work is the migration itself, and it is not a re-pin. A deployment holding Invocation records written under the old derivation cannot re-derive their ids from their inputs, so the fork needs either an explicit rewrite with durable migration-commit evidence under C13-RUN-EXPLICIT-MIGRATION's shape, or a recorded finding that no such deployment exists. I have established the latter only for facet.operation-descriptor itself (durability `value`, store `null`, no declared migration naming it); I have NOT established it for the InvocationId records the derivation names, and that is the open question.

The remaining eleven descriptor-digest sites are comparison-only or per-run: correspondence.ts:139-147 compares pinned declaration bytes within one install, authority.ts:236/257 compares an operationDigest captured and rechecked inside one resolution, executor.ts:161-162 likewise, and mediation-preparation.ts:344 / operation-mediation.ts:270 / canonical-batch.ts:798 / command-runtime.ts:391 record a descriptorDigest alongside the intent rather than deriving an identity from it. None forks an identity across restart; each still needs confirming against stored evidence before this row closes. My first version of this clause filed executor.ts:1463 here as "a descriptorDigest alongside an intent". It is not: it is the full descriptor inside a content-addressed record, and misfiling it is what hid the second fork for an hour. An enumeration is only as good as the reading of each entry, and the count was wrong in the direction that mattered.
